phrygian_agdistis.name: Engender Attis from the severed body
phrygian_agdistis.notes: Born androgyne from the rock Agdos (impregnated by the seed of Zeus/Papas); after the gods sever its male part, an almond (or pomegranate) springs up whose fruit impregnates the river-nymph Nana, who bears Attis.

sources.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.17.10-12; Arnobius, Adversus Nationes 5.5-7

phrygian_agdistis.name: Strike with frenzy and drive to self-mutilation
phrygian_agdistis.notes: Out of jealous love Agdistis maddens Attis at his wedding, causing him to castrate himself beneath the pine; the ecstatic frenzy of the cult's Galli re-enacts this power.

sources.reference: Arnobius, Adversus Nationes 5.5-7; Pausanias 7.17.10-12

polynesian_kanaloa.name: Heal the sick and counter sorcery
polynesian_kanaloa.notes: Prayers to Kanaloa are recited over the sick; with Kane he is invoked in kahuna healing to lift the effects of sorcery and disease.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Kane and Kanaloa)

polynesian_kanaloa.name: Open fresh-water springs with Kane
polynesian_kanaloa.notes: Travelling the islands with Kane in search of water and awa, the pair strike the ground to open freshwater springs (wai-a-Kane).

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Kane and Kanaloa)

polynesian_mahuika.name: Keep and yield fire from her fingernails and toenails
polynesian_mahuika.notes: The fire-goddess holds fire in her twenty nails; Maui tricks her into surrendering them one by one, and the last, hurled in rage, sets the world (and the fire-trees) alight.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (Maui and Mahuika); Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand

polynesian_mahuika.name: Plant fire in the wood of the kaikomako
polynesian_mahuika.notes: Her scattered fire lodges in the mahoe, totara, patete, pukatea and kaikomako trees, whence humankind thereafter draws fire by friction.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (Maui and Mahuika)

polynesian_hinenuitepo.name: Fix death upon humankind
polynesian_hinenuitepo.notes: By crushing Maui as he attempts to reverse mortality, the Great Lady of the Night makes him the first to die and seals death as the lot of all people.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (The Death of Maui)

pohnpeian_isokelekel.name: Lead the 333 from Katau against the Saudeleur
pohnpeian_isokelekel.notes: Born of the thunder-god, he musters 333 men, women and children, voyages from Katau (Eir/Kosrae), and storms Nan Madol to end the Saudeleur tyranny.

sources.reference: Hanlon, Upon a Stone Altar: A History of the Island of Pohnpei; Book of Luelen

phrygian_agdistis.name: Cult of the Mother at Pessinus (Agdistis)
phrygian_agdistis.cadence: ongoing, served by eunuch Galli priests
phrygian_agdistis.notes: At Pessinus the Mother of the Gods was titled Agdistis and worshipped in the form of a black meteoric stone; her castrated Galli served the shrine. The Roman embassy of 204 BCE fetched this Pessinuntine stone to Rome as the Magna Mater.

sources.reference: Strabo, Geography 12.5.3; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 29.10-14

phrygian_agdistis.name: Guardian cult of Agdistis at Philadelphia (Lydia)
phrygian_agdistis.notes: In the sacred law of the household sanctuary of Dionysios, Agdistis is set as the guardian (phylake) of the precinct, charged with watching over the moral oaths sworn by its members.

sources.reference: Sacred law of Dionysios, Philadelphia in Lydia (LSAM 20)

phoenician_resheph.name: Temple of Resheph-Apollo at Idalion
phoenician_resheph.cadence: civic cult of the Cypriote kingdom of Idalion
phoenician_resheph.notes: At Idalion on Cyprus Resheph was worshipped under the names ršp mkl and ršp ʾlyyt (Resheph of the heights), assimilated to Apollo; dedicatory inscriptions and votives mark his sanctuary as a leading Cypro-Phoenician cult of the plague-and-archer god.

sources.reference: Phoenician and trilingual votive inscriptions of Idalion (CIS I); Cypro-Phoenician temple of Reshef-Apollo

attributes.name: Androgynous (dual-sexed) primordial form
attributes.notes: Agdistis is figured as a being possessing both male and female generative organs, born of the earth-rock; its violent power leads the gods to unman it.

sources.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.17.10; Arnobius, Adversus Nationes 5.5

attributes.name: Aniconic black meteoric stone of Pessinus
attributes.notes: Where identified with the Pessinuntine Mother, Agdistis is embodied not in a statue but in an unworked black (meteoric) stone, the baetyl carried to Rome in 204 BCE.

sources.reference: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 29.11; Herodian 1.11

attributes.name: Octopus and squid body-form (kino lau)
attributes.notes: Kanaloa's bodily manifestations are the heʻe (octopus) and muheʻe (squid); in the Kumulipo he is Ka-heʻe-hauna-wela, 'the foul-smelling squid'.

sources.reference: Kumulipo (Hawaiian creation chant); Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology
Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (kino lau of Kanaloa)
Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Kane and Kanaloa as growers of banana)

sacredPlants.name: ʻAwa (kava)
sacredPlants.notes: Kanaloa is 'the awa-drinker'; awa is drunk with Kane and offered to him, and is invoked when consecrating a canoe for the sea.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Kanaloa the awa-drinker)

attributes.name: Conical sacred stone (Pohaku o Kane)
attributes.notes: Kane was worshipped at a single upright conical stone, the Pohaku o Kane, set up as a family altar; his rites were simple, without human sacrifice ('ua kapu ke ola na Kane', life is sacred to Kane).

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (the Kane worship; Pohaku o Kane)
Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Hawaiian kino lau tradition

sacredPlants.name: ʻAwa (kava)
sacredPlants.notes: Brought to Hawaiʻi and planted across the islands by Kane and Kanaloa; awa, mulberry and breadfruit are sacred to Kane.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (plants of Kane and Kanaloa)
Hawaiian kino lau tradition; Images of Old Hawaiʻi (gods who brought the plants)

attributes.name: Tapu garden-stones (whatu)
attributes.notes: Sacred stones representing Rongo were set in the kumara gardens to promote fertility; the first kumara of the harvest were buried as an offering to him.

sources.reference: Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand (kumara: religious aspects); Best, Maori Agriculture
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand (kumara and Rongo)

sacredPlants.name: Bracken fern-root (aruhe)
sacredPlants.notes: The edible rhizome of Pteridium esculentum is the body of Haumia; in the separation myth his hair, protruding from Papatuanuku, becomes the fern-root, and it is offered and acknowledged when wild food is gathered.

sources.reference: Tregear, The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand (Haumia-tiketike)

attributes.name: The woman seen in the moon, beating kapa
attributes.notes: Hina is identified with the figure in the moon (mahina derives from her name), where she perpetually beats out bark-cloth; her beater and anvil are sometimes said to be heard as thunder.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Hina who went to the moon)

sacredPlants.name: Paper-mulberry / banyan bark for kapa
sacredPlants.notes: Hina works the bark (wauke; in some tellings banyan) into the finest kapa cloth.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Hina the tapa-maker)

attributes.name: Teeth of obsidian and thighs set with flint and greenstone
attributes.notes: Her mouth is fanged with volcanic glass (obsidian) and her thighs hold sharp flakes of obsidian and greenstone (pounamu), with which she crushes Maui.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (The Death of Maui)

attributes.name: Eyes of greenstone, hair of kelp, mouth like a barracouta
attributes.notes: The standard portrait gives her eyes of pounamu (greenstone), hair of sea-kelp, and a mouth like that of the barracouta fish.

sources.reference: Te Ara / Maori oral tradition; recensions surveyed in scholarship on Hine-nui-te-po's form

sacredPlants.name: Kaikomako and mahoe fire-trees
sacredPlants.notes: Her scattered fire lodged in the kaikomako, mahoe, totara, patete and pukatea; dry kaikomako wood became the kindling-stick (kaunoti) for fire by friction.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (Maui and Mahuika)

attributes.name: Sea-water hurled to quench fire
attributes.notes: As goddess of the sea she pursues her sister Pele, raising tides and waves to extinguish the fires Pele opens in the earth.

sources.reference: Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (Pele and her sister Namakaokahai)

attributes.name: Mantle of white kapa (snow)
attributes.notes: Poliʻahu appears as a radiant woman robed in white kapa like fresh snow on Mauna Kea; in her contest with Pele she casts snow and mist to drive back the lava.

sources.reference: Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes (Pele and the Snow-goddess)

attributes.name: Rain and dew as tears of longing
attributes.notes: Separated from Papatuanuku, the sky-father weeps; his tears fall as rain and dew toward the earth, and her sighs rise back as mist.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (The Children of Heaven and Earth)

attributes.name: Rising mist as the sighs of the earth-mother
attributes.notes: Mist rising from forest and ground is the breath and longing of Papatuanuku for the sky-father from whom she was parted; her body nurtures all living things.

sources.reference: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (The Children of Heaven and Earth)

attributes.name: Basalt megaliths flown into place by magic
attributes.notes: With his brother Olisihpa, Olosohpa raised the prismatic basalt 'logs' of Nan Madol by incantation (in some tellings borne by a flying dragon), founding the stone city on the reef off Temwen.

sources.reference: Pohnpeian oral tradition of the founding of Nan Madol; Hanlon, Upon a Stone Altar
